entities.name: Silvanus of the Seventy
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Silvanus, often identified with Silas from the Acts of the Apostles, stands as a foundational figure within early Christian tradition, particularly venerated in Eastern Orthodoxy as one of the Seventy Apostles. While his birth and death dates remain unknown, his significance stems from his purported participation in the mission initiated by Jesus in Luke 10 and his explicit mention in the First Epistle of Peter (1 Peter 5:12). This dual connection firmly places him within the earliest stratum of Christian missionary activity and scriptural transmission, cementing his role as a bridge between the foundational apostolic era and the developing Church. His regional influence extended across the nascent Christian communities of Asia Minor, where Peter's epistle was directed, marking him as a crucial conduit for early theological instruction.

Tradition holds that Silvanus was among the seventy disciples commissioned by Jesus to precede him into 'every town and place where he himself was about to go,' proclaiming the Kingdom of God and performing healing miracles. This mission, described in Luke 10, represents an expansion of evangelistic efforts beyond the initial twelve apostles. More concretely, the First Epistle of Peter states, 'Through Silvanus, our faithful brother as I consider him, I have written to you briefly, exhorting and testifying that this is the true grace of God.' This verse strongly suggests Silvanus served as Peter's amanuensis or secretary, meticulously recording and perhaps even helping to shape the epistle's message of steadfast faith amidst persecution, likely penned in Rome between 60-64 CE.
